a variety of samples,

& tree bark.
Cell Theory

Antonie Van 
Leeuwenhoek
• 1632 - 1723
• self taught amateur 
naturalist
• often credited as creating 
the first microscope
• first to observe bacteria & 
protists

Robert Hooke
• 1635 - 1703
• published ‘Micrographia’ 
in 1665
• examined thin slices of 
cork

compartments, which he

Cell Theory

Mattias Schleiden 
• 1804 - 1881
• Lawyer & botanist
• concluded that all 
plants are composed

Cell Theory

Theodor Schwann 
• 1810 - 1882

• concluded that all animal

Cell Theory

Rudolf Virchow
• 1821 - 1902

Cell Theory

Cell Theory has 3 tenets:
All living organisms consist of one or more 
cells
The cell is the basic unit of structure for all 
organisms
All cells only arise from pre-existing cells

• A cell is the simplest unit of 
living matter.
• There are 2 general categories 
of cells:
⚬ prokaryotic
⚬ eukaryotic

Prokaryotic cells
• pro = early, primitive, before
• kary = genes, refers to DNA / 
RNA (ie. nucleus)
• These are simple, small cells 
• they lack a nucleus and 
membrane-bound organelles.

Prokaryotic cells
• Bacteria & cyanobacteria 
(unicellular algae) are examples 
• These cells have DNA & RNA 
loose in the cytoplasm.
• 3 common shapes are cocci 
(round), bacilli (rod), spirillum 
(wavy or spiral)
Prokaryotic cells

Eukaryotic cells
• eu = true, real
• Multicellular algae, protozoans, 
fungi, plants & animals are all 
composed of eukaryotic cells.

Eukaryotic cells
• These cells are significantly larger & 
structurally more complex than 
prokaryotes.  
• They all contain membrane-bound 
organelles (specialized structures that 
perform specific functions)

Flagella & Cilia
• Usually one (flagellum), 
• or a few (flagella), 
• long projections, used for 
locomotion
• are external projections 
used for cell locomotion,
• or for moving substances 
along the surface of a cell.  
• They are made of tubules of 
protein. 
• Usually numerous cilia
• short projections
• cover all or a portion of the cell

Cell Wall
• provides support & protection to 
the cell.
• Algae & plants -   cell wall is made 
of cellulose (β glucose chains)
• Fungi – cell wall is made of chitin

Cell Membrane
• selectively allows materials to pass in & out of the cell.  
• is the outer living boundary of the cell.
• is made of phospholipids & proteins

cytoplasm
• cyto =  cell, plasm = goop
• Cytoplasm includes everything inside the cell 
membrane & outside the nucleus.  
• made up of fluid (H2O) & the cytoskeleton
• provides shape & support to the cell.  
• Movement of the fluid, called cytoplasmic 
streaming, helps disperse nutrients 
throughout the cell. 
Cytoplasm

Nucleus
• usually spherical or oval,
• often the largest structure inside a cell
• contains the cell’s hereditary information 
(DNA),
• separated from the cytoplasm by a double 
membrane.  
• fluid inside the nucleus is called 
nucleoplasm.  
• also contains nucleoli, the site of ribosome 
production, 
• and DNA & proteins in the form of 
chromatin or chromosomes.
Nucleus

smooth ER
rough ER
Endoplasmic Reticulum
• A system of pairs of parallel membranes that enclose 
narrow cavities, the ER forms a network of canals.  
• It is continuous with the cell membrane and the 
nuclear membrane.  
• Lipids (fats) are made here, and proteins (made at 
ribosomes) are transported here.  
• The ER provides a surface area for chemical 
reactions, a pathway for the transport of molecules, 
and a storage area for synthesized molecules.
• There are 2 types of ER: 
⚬ Smooth (SER) lacks ribosomes
⚬ Rough (RER) lined with ribosomes

• are NOT membrane bound. 
• These small, dense, spherical bodies are made of 
strands of rRNA (ribosomal RNA).  
• Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis 
• They are found free in the cytoplasm, attached to 
RER, or as polysomes.
 
A polysome = a cluster of ribosomes.  This provides a 
site for the production of proteins needed within a 
cell.
 
Ribosomes
ribosomes

Golgi
• Golgi consist of 4-8 flattened disks, 
called  ‘cisternae’, 
• which bulge at the ends to bud off 
spherical vesicles.
• Golgi may sometimes connect to ER, 
• it’s function is to package & secrete 
proteins, lipids, & carbohydrates.
Golgi body

• These small organelles are bean-shaped,                                         filamentous & 
appear throughout the cytoplasm. 
• Mitochondria have a double membrane system                                  enclosing a 
fluid-filled matrix.  
• The outer membrane is smooth, while the inner is                                      highly 
convoluted.
• This provides a large surface area for the reactions of cellular respiration:
The mitochondria produced adenosine triphosphate (ATP), which is the energy 
currency of cells.
Mitochondria

• all are membrane enclosed spheres 
used to store or transport materials in 
cells.
• Vacuoles – large compartments
• Vesicles – tiny compartments  
• Lysosomes – specialized compartments 
that are filled with digestive 
(proteolytic) enzymes.
vesicles & vacuoles

chloroplasts
• Chloroplasts are unique to algae & 
plant cells.
• These membranous structures contain 
chlorophyll & the enzymes needed for 
photosynthesis in stacks called 
‘thylakoids’. 
chloroplasts
outer membrane
inner membrane thylakoid

Membrane Structure:
The cell membrane is made of a double layer of phospholipid 
molecules with proteins scattered throughout.

Membrane Structure:
• Phospholipids have a hydrophilic phosphate end, and a hydrophobic lipid 
end.
⚬ hydro= water      philia = loving      phobia = fearing
• When placed in water, the lipids align together in the middle, sandwiched by 
the phosphates, to form a bilayer.  
• There are also proteins & cholesterol found within the membrane.

The membrane is described as a Fluid Mosaic model, because:
• Fluid - the component parts are able to move or flow laterally
• Mosaic - the membrane is made of different parts, like a mosaic
Protein
Cholesterol
Phospholipids

Membranes are semi-permeable
• they permit some molecules to pass through, but 
prevent or slow others. 
• Small Molecules: can pass through freely   
• Large Molecules: generally prevented from 
passing.  
• Some may move through pores or channels.

Passive 
Transport
• most small molecules cross the membrane by 
diffusion.  
• They will naturally flow from an area of high 
concentration to one of low concentration. 
• due to the inherent energy possessed by all molecules 
• No additional energy is required for diffusion to occur
high
concentration
low
concentration

Passive 
Transport
• Some molecules diffuse only though specific 
membrane protein channels.  
• This is called facilitated diffusion.
simple diffusion
facilitated 
transport

Factors affecting diffusion rate:
• Temperature - molecules move faster at higher temperatures, 
so diffusion would accelerate.
• Size - smaller molecules diffuse faster than larger ones.
• Charge - neutral molecules freely pass through cell 
membranes, but charged molecules are often blocked.
• Concentration gradient – the higher the concentration 
difference, the faster diffusion occurs.

• The movement of water across membranes by 
diffusion is called osmosis
• Water will move in an attempt to equilibrate.
• Isotonic  = the same concentration inside the cell 
as outside.  Molecules enter & leave the cell at the 
same rate.
• Hypertonic = more concentrated outside. Water 
leaves the cell & it shrivels
• Hypotonic = less concentrated outside.  Water 
enters the cell & it swells
Osmosis

• to move molecules against a concentration gradient (from an 
area of lower concentration to one of higher concentration)
• to move large molecules across the membrane. (proteins, 
hormones, enzymes)
• Cellular energy, in the form of  ATP is used.   
• ATP =  Adenosine Tri Phosphate
Active transport uses energy

Forms of 
Active 
Transport
• Phagocytosis = cell eating.  This is when the cell 
engulfs a large particle, creating a vacuole.
• Pinocytosis = cell drinking. This is when small droplets move into 
the cell, creating vesicles
• Exocytosis/secretion= opposite of phago/pinocytosis.  Material produced 
in the cell is moved to the outside.
• protein pumps = specialized protein molecules embedded in the 
membrane move materials across, using energy (ATP) in the process.

• Membranes surrounding organelles is identical to the cell 
membrane.  
• It is composed of a phospholipid bilayer, with proteins & cholesterol 
embedded within.
• Due to endo & exocytosis, segments of membranes within cells can 
interchange: 
• Membrane that begins as endoplasmic reticulum can pinch off as a 
vacuole and then migrate & fuse to the golgi.
organelle membranes

• The cell membrane determines how much material can enter and leave a 
cell.   
• The size of the membrane (surface area) determines the rate of transport of 
materials. 
• The cytoplasm determines how much food the cell needs & how much waste 
it produces (volume).
• Mathematically, these two factors do not increase at the same rate. 
surface area: volume ratio

• As the cell grows, its volume increases at a faster rate than its 
surface area. 
• This means that the volume (amount of cytoplasm) outgrows the 
surface area’s (cell membrane’s) ability to bring in nutrients & 
remove wastes to keep the cell alive.  
• At this point, the cell will either need to divide, or it will die.
